newsitem.title: USA: Hate crime experts doubt bomb letter's authorship.
newsitem.headline: Hate crime experts doubt bomb letter's authorship.

text.p: Hate crime experts expressed doubt Tuesday that an anonymous letter claiming responsibility for two recent Atlanta bombings had been the work of the Army of God, as the letter stated.

The three-page handwritten letter, received by several news organisations including Reuters, said the group of Christian anti-abortion activists had carried out bombings on a gay and lesbian nightclub last Friday and on an Atlanta abortion clinic in January.
As pictures of the document flashed across television screens, Jewish and civil rights groups tightened security for fear of another attack.
The letter, postmarked Saturday, claimed to describe details of the nightclub bomb's makeup which were not generally known at the time.
More disturbing for crime experts, however, was a section which laid out a code system for identifying claims of responsibility for future bombings.

Some said it could be the first time that a domestic group had taken such an elaborate step. Up to now, identification codes have been associated solely with foreign organisations, including the Irish Republican Army.

Hate experts said that was one reason to doubt the bombings had been carried out by the Army of God, a declining organisation whose membership has dwindled to little more than a dozen. More likely was a small cell of extremists influenced by the racist theologies of Christian Identity groups and the Phineas Priesthood, they said.

"My feeling is the Army of God hasn't been that much of a factor. All of a sudden for them to appear out of nowhere is kind of surprising. It doesn't quite all seem to fit," said Jay Kaiman, Atlanta director of the Anti-Defamation League.
In Washington, Attorney General Janet Reno denounced the bombing last weekend at a predominantly lesbian nightclub called The Otherside as "another despicable act of domestic terrorism."
But some were not so sure how much protection the federal government could provide in a city that has been struck by three bombings in seven months.

"It happened and it's going to happen again and next time it may be a completely different issue-area. It may be an attack on a Jewish synagogue or a black church," said Noah Chandler of the Centre for Democratic Studies.

The Klanwatch Project of the Southern Poverty Law Centre in Montgomery, Ala., said the bombings could be the work of a group influenced by Christian Identity, an ideology that describes whites as God's chosen people and violently opposes abortion, homosexuals, Jews and racial minorities.

After reviewing excerpts of the letter, the Klanwatch's senior intelligence analyst, Mike Reynolds, said the language was unusual for the Army of God because it lacked the organisation's customary Army of God references to the Bible.

Reynolds seized on two passages from the letter, the warning: "anyone in or around facilities that murder children may become victims of retribution," and in a reference to "the policy of ungodly preversion (sic) that's destroying our people."
"It sounds authentic," said Reynolds, who compiles data on hate group activities and disseminates the information to law enforcement agencies nationwide.
"They're seeking to establish themselves as an authentic revolutionary presence, an insurgency presence. 'Retribution' is key. 'Our people' is key."

By contrast, the Phineas Priesthood takes its justification for murder from Old Testament hero Phineas, who served Yahweh by slaying an Israelite and a Midianite whose interracial union had brought a plague upon Israel.
Both groups believe themselves to be waging a holy war against what they call the new world order.
